title: II. Dangerous Witnesses
paragraphs: I can’t say whether the President split the witnesses for the defense and for the prosecution into groups, or arranged to call them in any set order. No doubt he did. All I know is that the witnesses for the prosecution came first. Again, I don’t mean to go through the questioning step by step. My account would be partly pointless anyway, because the speeches for the prosecution and for the defense pulled the whole course of the evidence together and showed it in a strong, telling light. I took down parts of those two remarkable speeches in full, and I will quote them in their place. I will also tell of one extraordinary and quite unexpected episode that came before the final speeches, and that surely helped bring about the sinister, fatal outcome of the trial.

I will only point out one odd feature of the case that was plain to everyone from the first moments of the trial: the prosecution was overwhelmingly stronger than anything the defense had to lean on. Everyone saw it as soon as the facts began to gather around a single point and the whole horrible, bloody crime came gradually into view. Perhaps everyone felt from the start that the case was beyond dispute, that there was no doubt in it, that there could really be no argument, that the defense was a mere formality, and that the prisoner was guilty, plainly and conclusively guilty. I imagine that even the ladies, so impatient to see the interesting prisoner acquitted, were all of them, at the same time, convinced of his guilt. What’s more, I believe they would have been mortified if his guilt had not been so firmly proved, because that would have weakened the effect of the closing scene, when the criminal is acquitted. Strange to say, all the ladies were firmly sure right up to the last moment that he would be acquitted. “He is guilty, but he will be acquitted, out of humanity, in keeping with the new ideas and the new feelings that have come into fashion,” and so on, and so on. That was why they had crowded into the court so eagerly. The men cared more about the contest between the prosecutor and the famous Fetyukovitch. They kept asking themselves what even a talent like Fetyukovitch’s could make of such a hopeless case, and so they followed his every move with close attention.

Yet Fetyukovitch stayed a riddle to everyone until the very end, until his speech. Experienced people suspected that he had a design, that he was working toward some aim, but it was almost impossible to guess what. His confidence and self-reliance were unmistakable, though. Everyone noticed, too, and was pleased, that after so short a stay among us, perhaps no more than three days, he had mastered the case so wonderfully and “had studied it to the last detail.” Afterward people described with relish how cleverly he had “taken down” all the witnesses for the prosecution. He had confused them as much as he could and, what’s more, had smeared their reputations and so lowered the worth of their evidence. But people supposed he did this rather as sport, so to speak, for professional glory, to show that none of the accepted methods had been skipped. They were all convinced that blackening the witnesses like this could do him no real good, and that he knew it better than anyone. They thought he had some idea of his own in reserve, some hidden weapon of defense, which he would spring on us when the time came. Meanwhile, sure of his strength, he seemed to be amusing himself.

For example, when Grigory, Fyodor Pavlovitch’s old servant, gave evidence, the counsel for the defense simply pounced on him when his turn to ask questions came. Grigory was the one who had given the most damning testimony about the open door. It should be said that he walked into the hall calm and almost stately, not in the least put off by the majesty of the court or the huge audience listening to him. He gave his evidence as confidently as if he were chatting with his Marfa, only perhaps more respectfully. There was no making him contradict himself. The prosecutor questioned him first, at length, about the family life of the Karamazovs. The family portrait came out in lurid colors. You could see and hear that the witness was honest and fair. Despite his deep reverence for his dead master’s memory, he still testified that the old man had been unjust to Mitya and “hadn’t brought up his children as he should. He’d have been eaten alive by lice when he was little, if it hadn’t been for me,” he added, speaking of Mitya’s early childhood. “It wasn’t right either, a father cheating his son over his mother’s property, which was his by rights.”

The prosecutor asked what grounds he had for saying that Fyodor Pavlovitch had wronged his son in money matters. To everyone’s surprise, Grigory had no proof whatever to offer. Still, he insisted that the settlement with the son was “unfair” and that the father ought “to have paid him several thousand roubles more.” I should mention, by the way, that the prosecutor pressed this question, whether Fyodor Pavlovitch had really held back part of Mitya’s inheritance, on every witness who could be asked it, Alyosha and Ivan included. But he got no exact information from anyone. All said it was so, and none could produce any clear proof. Grigory’s account of the scene at the dinner table, when Dmitri burst in, beat his father and threatened to come back and kill him, left a sinister impression on the court. The old servant told it calmly, sparing his words, in his own odd way of speaking, and that was as effective as eloquence. He said he was not angry with Mitya for knocking him down and hitting him in the face. He had forgiven him long ago. Of the late Smerdyakov he said, crossing himself, that he was a gifted lad, but stupid and afflicted, and, worse still, a godless one, and that Fyodor Pavlovitch and his elder son had taught him to be so. But he defended Smerdyakov’s honesty almost warmly. He told how Smerdyakov had once found the master’s money in the yard and, instead of hiding it, had carried it to his master. The master had given him a “gold piece” for it and trusted him completely from then on. He insisted stubbornly that the garden door had been open. But he was asked so many questions that I can’t remember them all.

At last the counsel for the defense began his cross-examination. His first question concerned the envelope in which Fyodor Pavlovitch was supposed to have put three thousand roubles for “a certain person.” “Did you ever see it, you who attended your master so closely for so many years?” Grigory answered that he had not seen it, and had never heard of the money from anyone “till everybody was talking about it.” Fetyukovitch asked this question about the envelope of everyone who could conceivably have known of it, just as persistently as the prosecutor asked his about Dmitri’s inheritance, and he got the same answer from all: nobody had seen the envelope, though many had heard of it. From the beginning everyone noticed how Fetyukovitch kept coming back to this subject.

“Now, if you’ll allow me, I’ll ask you something,” Fetyukovitch said, suddenly and unexpectedly. “What was that balsam made of—or rather that decoction—which, as we learn from the preliminary inquiry, you rubbed on your lumbago that evening, hoping to cure it?”
Grigory stared blankly at him. After a short silence he muttered, “There was saffron in it.”
“Only saffron? You don’t remember anything else in it?”
“Milfoil, too.”
“And pepper, maybe?” Fetyukovitch asked.
“Yes, pepper too.”
“And so on. And all of it dissolved in vodka?”
“In spirit.”
A faint ripple of laughter ran through the court.
“You see, in spirit. And after rubbing your back, I believe, you drank what was left in the bottle, saying a certain pious prayer that only your wife knows?”
“I did.”
“Did you drink much? A glass or two, roughly?”
“Could have been a tumblerful.”
“A tumblerful, then. Maybe a tumbler and a half?”
Grigory didn’t answer. He seemed to see what was being aimed at.
“A glass and a half of neat spirit—not bad at all, is it? You could see the gates of heaven open, not just the door into the garden?”
Grigory kept silent. Again there was laughter in the court. The President shifted in his seat.
“And do you know for certain,” Fetyukovitch pressed on, “whether you were awake or not when you saw the open door?”
“I was standing up.”
“That doesn’t prove you were awake.” (Again there was laughter in the court.) “If someone had asked you a question at that moment, could you have answered it? What year it is, for instance?”
“I don’t know.”
“And what year is it, Anno Domini? Do you know?”
Grigory stood there bewildered, looking straight at his tormentor. Strange to say, he really did seem not to know the year.
“Then perhaps you can tell me how many fingers you have on your hands?”
“I am a servant,” Grigory said suddenly, in a loud, clear voice. “If my betters want to make sport of me, it is my duty to bear it.”

Fetyukovitch was slightly taken aback. The President stepped in and told him to keep his questions to the point. Fetyukovitch bowed with dignity and said he had nothing more to ask the witness. Of course, the public and the jury were left with a grain of doubt about a man who, while undergoing a certain cure, might have seen “the gates of heaven,” and who did not even know what year he lived in. But before Grigory left the stand, there was another episode. The President turned to the prisoner and asked if he wished to comment on the last witness’s evidence.

“All of it is true, except what he says about the door,” Mitya cried loudly. “I thank him for combing the lice off me, and I thank him for forgiving my blows. The old man has been honest all his life, and as faithful to my father as seven hundred poodles.”
“Prisoner, watch your language,” the President warned him.
“I am not a poodle,” Grigory muttered.
“Fine, I’m the poodle myself,” cried Mitya. “If it’s an insult, I’ll take it on myself, and I beg his pardon. I was a beast to him, and cruel. I was cruel to Æsop too.”
“What Æsop?” the President asked sternly again.
“Oh, Pierrot ... my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
Again and again the President warned Mitya, very sternly and with great force, to watch his language.
“You are hurting yourself in the eyes of your judges.”

The counsel for the defense dealt just as cleverly with Rakitin’s evidence. I may say that Rakitin was one of the leading witnesses, and the prosecutor set great store by him. It turned out that he knew everything. His knowledge was amazing. He had been everywhere, seen everything, talked to everybody, and knew every detail of the lives of Fyodor Pavlovitch and all the Karamazovs. He had heard of the envelope, it is true, only from Mitya himself. But he described Mitya’s exploits at the “Metropolis” in minute detail, with all the compromising things he had done and said, and he told the story of Captain Snegiryov’s “wisp of tow.” Yet even Rakitin could say nothing definite about Mitya’s inheritance, and he kept to contemptuous generalities.

“Who could tell which of them was to blame, and which owed the other money, with their crazy Karamazov way of muddling things so that no one could make head or tail of it?” He put the tragic crime down to habits ingrained by ages of serfdom and to the sorry state of Russia, which he blamed on the lack of proper institutions. He was, in fact, allowed a good deal of freedom to speak. This was the first time Rakitin showed what he could do and drew notice. The prosecutor knew that the witness was preparing a magazine article on the case. Later, in his speech, as we shall see, he quoted some ideas from that article, which showed he had already seen it. The picture the witness painted was a gloomy, sinister one, and it greatly strengthened the case for the prosecution. Altogether, Rakitin’s talk fascinated the public by its independence and the remarkable nobility of its ideas. There were even two or three bursts of applause when he spoke of serfdom and the sorry state of Russia.

But Rakitin, in his youthful ardor, made a small blunder, and the counsel for the defense seized on it at once, with great skill. He was answering some questions about Grushenka. Carried away by the loftiness of his own feelings and by his success, of which he was of course aware, he went so far as to speak rather contemptuously of Agrafena Alexandrovna as “the kept mistress of Samsonov.” Later he would have paid a good deal to take those words back, for Fetyukovitch caught him out on them immediately. And it was all because Rakitin had not reckoned that the lawyer could have learned every detail so thoroughly in so short a time.

“Allow me to ask,” the counsel for the defense began, with the friendliest and even respectful smile, “you are, of course, the same Mr. Rakitin whose pamphlet, _The Life of the Deceased Elder, Father Zossima_, published by the diocesan authorities, full of deep and religious reflections and opening with an excellent, devout dedication to the bishop, I have just read with such pleasure?”
“I didn’t write it for publication ... it was published afterward,” muttered Rakitin, for some reason badly rattled and almost ashamed.

“Oh, excellent! A thinker like you can, and indeed ought to, take the widest view of every social question. Your most instructive pamphlet has circulated widely thanks to the bishop’s patronage, and has been of real use.... But here is the main thing I’d like to learn from you. You said just now that you were very well acquainted with Madame Svyetlov.” (It should be noted that Grushenka’s surname was Svyetlov. I heard it for the first time that day, during the trial.)
“I can’t answer for all my acquaintances.... I’m a young man ... and who can be responsible for everyone he meets?” cried Rakitin, turning red all over.

“I understand, I quite understand,” cried Fetyukovitch, as if he too were embarrassed and hurrying to make excuses. “You, like anyone, might well be interested in knowing a young and beautiful woman who would gladly receive the _élite_ of the young men of the neighborhood. But ... I only wanted to know ... It has come to my knowledge that a couple of months ago Madame Svyetlov was particularly eager to meet the younger Karamazov, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and promised you twenty-five roubles if you would bring him to her in his monastic dress. And that actually happened, on the evening of the very day when the terrible crime now under investigation was committed. You brought Alexey Karamazov to Madame Svyetlov, and did you receive the twenty-five roubles from her as a reward? That is what I wanted to hear from you.”
“It was a joke.... I don’t see how it could interest you.... I took it as a joke ... meaning to give it back later....”
“Then you did take— But you haven’t given it back yet ... or have you?”
“That doesn’t matter,” muttered Rakitin. “I refuse to answer such questions.... Of course I’ll give it back.”

The President stepped in, but Fetyukovitch declared he had no more questions for the witness. Mr. Rakitin left the witness box with his character not altogether free of stain. The effect of the lofty idealism of his speech was rather spoiled. Fetyukovitch’s expression, as he watched him go, seemed to say to the public, “Here is a sample of the high-minded people who accuse him.” I remember that this incident too did not pass without an outburst from Mitya. He was furious at the tone in which Rakitin had spoken of Grushenka, and he suddenly shouted “Bernard!” After Rakitin’s cross-examination, the President asked the prisoner whether he had anything to say, and Mitya cried out loudly:
“Since I’ve been arrested, he has borrowed money from me! He is a contemptible Bernard and an opportunist, and he doesn’t believe in God. He fooled the bishop!”

Mitya, of course, was called to order again for his wild language, but Rakitin was finished. Captain Snegiryov’s evidence was a failure too, though for quite a different reason. He turned up in ragged, dirty clothes and muddy boots, and despite the vigilance and trained eyes of the police officers, he proved to be hopelessly drunk. Asked about Mitya’s attack on him, he refused to answer.
“God bless him. Ilusha told me not to. God will make it up to me yonder.”
“Who told you not to tell? Who are you talking about?”
“Ilusha, my little son. ‘Father, father, how he insulted you!’ He said that by the stone. Now he is dying....”
The captain suddenly burst into sobs and dropped to his knees before the President. He was hustled out amid laughter from the public. The effect the prosecutor had prepared did not come off at all.

Fetyukovitch went on making the most of every chance, and amazed people more and more with his detailed knowledge of the case. Trifon Borissovitch, for example, made a great impression, of course, and a very damaging one for Mitya. He worked out almost on his fingers that on his first visit to Mokroe Mitya must have spent three thousand roubles, “or very little less. Just think what he squandered on those gypsy girls alone! And as for our lousy peasants, it wasn’t a matter of tossing half a rouble into the street. He gave them presents of twenty-five roubles each, at the least. He gave no less than that. And how much money was simply stolen from him! And if anyone did steal, he left no receipt. How could you catch the thief, when he was throwing his money away the whole time? Our peasants are robbers, you know. They have no thought for their souls. And the way he carried on with the girls, our village girls! They’re set up since then, I tell you. They used to be poor.” He recalled, in fact, every item of expense and added it all up. So the theory that only fifteen hundred had been spent, and the rest put away in a little bag, seemed impossible to believe.
“I saw three thousand in his hands, as plain as day. I saw it with my own eyes. I should think I know how to count money,” cried Trifon Borissovitch, doing his best to please “his betters.”

When Fetyukovitch came to cross-examine him, he hardly tried to refute his evidence. Instead he began asking him about an incident at the first carousal at Mokroe, a month before the arrest. Timofey and another peasant, Akim, had picked up from the floor of the passage a hundred roubles that Mitya had dropped while drunk. They had handed it to Trifon Borissovitch, and he had given each of them a rouble for it. “Well,” asked the lawyer, “did you give that hundred roubles back to Mr. Karamazov?” Trifon Borissovitch squirmed in vain.... Once the peasants had been examined, he had to admit that the hundred roubles had been found. He only added that he had scrupulously given all of it back to Dmitri Fyodorovitch “in perfect honesty, and it’s only because his honor was in liquor at the time that he wouldn’t remember it.” But he had denied the incident of the hundred roubles until the peasants were called to prove it, so his evidence about returning the money to Mitya was naturally viewed with great suspicion. And so one of the most dangerous witnesses brought forward by the prosecution was discredited once more.

The same thing happened with the Poles. They took a proud, independent stand. They shouted loudly that they had both served the Crown, that “Pan Mitya” had offered them three thousand “to buy their honor,” and that they had seen a large sum of money in his hands. Pan Mussyalovitch stuffed a terrible number of Polish words into his sentences. He saw that this only raised his standing with the President and the prosecutor, so he grew more and more pompous and ended by speaking Polish altogether. But Fetyukovitch caught them in his snares too. Trifon Borissovitch was called back and, despite his dodging, was forced to admit that Pan Vrublevsky had swapped in a different pack of cards for the one he had provided, and that Pan Mussyalovitch had cheated during the game. Kalganov confirmed this, and both Poles left the witness box with their reputations damaged, amid laughter from the public.

Then exactly the same thing happened with almost all the most dangerous witnesses. Fetyukovitch managed to put a stain on every one of them and send them off with a touch of mockery. The lawyers and experts were lost in admiration. They only could not see what good purpose it served, since everyone, I repeat, felt that the case for the prosecution could not be refuted, but was growing more and more tragically overwhelming. Yet from the confidence of the “great magician” they could see that he was serene, and they waited. They felt that “such a man” had not come from Petersburg for nothing, and that he was not a man to go home unsuccessful.
